title: Crosslink variability fingerprinting and microburst profiling
body:
Summary:

This is a working note describing an empirical "fingerprinting" approach we used to surface cross-link variability and microburst-driven tail events in multi-GPU LLM inference. The emphasis is on repeatable experiments that isolate NIC/PCIe/NVLink behavior, NCCL fallback triggers, and host staging interactions for small-interleaved request workloads.

Why this felt necessary:
- Many production tail incidents are non-deterministic and only reproduce under particular mixes of small requests with KV-cache replays.
- Existing traces point to link-level variance (temporary drops in effective bandwidth) but we lacked an experiment that consistently reproduces the signature across topologies.
- We want concrete mitigation knobs (pacing, queueing, topology hints) rather than vague suggestions.

High-level hypothesis:
1) Microbursts from host staging + small-packet interleaving cause transient link saturation on particular NVLink/PCIe paths which increases collective latency and sometimes forces NCCL into a fallback path.
2) The fallback (p2p->rdma or falling back to host-based collectives) increases tail latency by 2-6x for affected steps.
3) Injecting deterministic pacing at staging or smoothing the request burst reduces the frequency of fallback triggers and cuts tail p99/p999 by significant margins.

Testbed and topology notes:
- Cluster: 4 x nodes, each node: 8x A100-80GB (connected with NVLink on-node and 2x HDR100 IB per node for cross-node).
- Switch fabrics: leaf spine with mixed Mellanox HDR100 and some older HDR200 spares in lab (we note differences below).
- Kernel: Ubuntu 22.04 + driver 510.y + OFED 5.4; NCCL v2.14 (with extended logging enabled via NCCL_DEBUG=WARN,NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=ALL during runs).
- Workloads: GPT-like transformer 30B (sharded as TP=2, PP=4 across 8 GPUs), and a smaller 6B model for short runs.
- Request patterns: small interactive requests (avg length 12 tokens), synthetic KV-cache replay bursts, and a synthetic streaming interleave generator which issues 64 concurrent 1-token continuation requests (to emulate a chat fanout).

Fingerprinting methodology (how we make the problem reproducible):
- Deterministic seeds in client harness to ensure identical request arrival order across trials.
- Repeated runs (n=50) per pattern and topology with 30s cool-down between runs to let NIC buffers flush and thermal effects settle.
- Capture NIC counters (ib_read_counters, ib_write_counters), kernel ring stats (ethtool -S output), per-GPU NVLink counters (nvidia-smi dmon + nouveau perf counters where available), and NCCL trace logs per rank.
- Lightweight packet capture at host NIC (tcpdump -w) restricted to small window around measured tail events (automatic trigger when step latency > baseline + 3 sigma).
- A local synthetic injector (trace-replay binary) that can replay recorded host-side enqueue timing with microsecond-level fidelity.

Representative observations:
1) Reproducible microburst signature: when the serving harness emits simultaneous small worklets to multiple GPUs, we see short (1.2-4ms) drops in per-link throughput on a subset of NVLink lanes; these align with microsecond-aligned host staging peaks.
2) NCCL fallback correlation: in ~18% of affected runs the collective reported an "incomplete ring" followed by a log entry signaling fallback to tree-based algorithm. The NCCL logs show packet reassembly retries followed by a longer barrier (200-600ms extra for the step).
3) Topology-specific behavior: nodes with mixed NVLink generation (some GPUs with fewer links due to topology mismatch) exhibited higher fallback frequency. On fully homogeneous boxes the frequency dropped by ~3x.
4) PCIe read amplification: when KV-cache replay is active and host staging is heavy, we see elevated PCIe read latencies and increased read amplification counters; these align with longer tail on small requests.
5) Buffering impacts: the presence of an on-host software queue (our staging thread) with bursty dispatch exacerbates the microburst; changing the staging thread to a leaky-bucket paced dispatcher reduced fallback frequency by ~70% in these tests.

Quick numbers (p99/p999 delta examples):
- Baseline (no synthetic bursts): p99 step = 35ms, p999 = 120ms.
- Burst (unpaced): p99 = 120ms, p999 = 560ms.
- Burst + staging pacing (software leaky bucket): p99 = 48ms, p999 = 160ms.
- Burst + kernel NIC interrupt affinity tuned + qdisc fq_codel smoothing: p99 = 42ms, p999 = 140ms.
(These numbers are illustrative from the 30B experiments on the testbed above.)

Short postmortem on an example run (timestamped markers):
- t=0: client fires 64 concurrent 1-token requests clustered within 300us.
- t=0.4ms: host staging threads push work to GPUs; several GPUs begin DMA reads from host (PCIe).
- t=1.2ms: NVLink lane A throughput drops ~40% for ~2ms window; NVLink lane B unaffected.
- t=3.6ms: NCCL ring step fails progress checks -> fallback triggered -> extra barrier introduced.
- t=300-600ms: overall inference step finishes for affected minibatch; other minibatches completed much earlier.

Mitigation ideas tried to date (and immediate results):
- Software pacing at staging: large improvement, cheap. Risk: increases median latency slightly if over-throttled.
- NIC interrupt/coalescing tuning + irqbalance settings: reduced noisy candidate nodes p999 by ~15-25%.
- qdisc (fq_codel) on host for transporter queue smoothing: small benefit, helps at p99 but not p999 unless combined with pacing.
- Preferential topology placement hinting: placing peers to avoid mixing GPUs with reduced NVLink connectivity halved fallback incidents in this hardware set.
- NCCL parameter tuning (ring chunk size, algorithm selection hints): mitigates some cases but can harm throughput when no microburst present.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Need a microsecond-accurate NIC buffer occupancy metric; current OFED counters are coarse. Explore adding Mellanox telemetry hooks.
- How do these findings change with HDR200 vs HDR100 vs new ethernet options? Run same fingerprint on cloud provider machines for cross-vendor validation.
- Can we bake a pacing suggestion into Redwood Optimize as an automatic mitigation when small-request interleaving is detected?
- Investigate kernel-bypass NIC drivers (e.g., DPDK) for staging path to avoid kernel qdisc jitter.
- Explore dynamic NCCL algo selection that uses a recent link-variance score to prefer algorithms resilient to microbursts.

Experiment artifacts and reproducibility notes:
- I dropped trace-replay scripts into github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/tools/trace-replay (see PR above). The harness needs to be run with NCCL_DEBUG=INFO and the provided collect-counters.sh wrapper.
- Use the annotated run script (runs/2025-02-14/fingerprint-*) which bundles kernel params and NIC settings used for each run. These are linked in the PR.

Concluding thoughts:
- This feels actionable: the combo of pacing + placement heuristics buys most of the tail reduction with minimal infra change.
- We should keep chasing better link telemetry and cross-vendor validation before recommending aggressive parameter flips for Dedicated/Private customers.

Notes to self: add a short reproducible checklist for SRE on-call to run when customers report intermittent p99 regressions that look like "sudden ring stalls". Also schedule an async sync with platform-engineering to discuss embedding a lightweight pacing shim into the staging thread used by our runtime.

References and quick links:
- JIRA-7891: "Intermittent ring fallback during small request storms"
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/412 (trace-replay + collect counters)
- Confluence draft: link-variability-playbook (internal)

End of note.

(If anyone wants to run the harness I can attach the run script and a minimal VM image snapshot. — Asha)
